newsitem.title: GERMANY: Significant number ready for EMU in 97--Luxembourg.
newsitem.headline: Significant number ready for EMU in 97--Luxembourg.

text.p: Luxembourg premier Jean-Claude Juncker on Thursday said he thought a "signficant" number of countries would meet the European Monetary Union criteria in 1997.

Speaking in Bonn, Juncker said the budget deficit criteria in the Maastricht treaty, which require would-be members to limit budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), should be read as three percent, not 3.0 percent.
"The three in the (Maastricht treaty) should be interpreted in terms of trend," Juncker said.
"If (German finance minister) Theo Waigel had said 3.8 (percent) was also okay, countries would never have made the strict effort," Juncker said.

Juncker went on say that he thought the European Central Bank (ECB), which is officially due to take over the operations of the European Monetary Institute when the euro starts in 1999, must be an independent body.
"The independence of the future ECB must not be interfered with," he said.
A stability pact was necessary, but having a stability pact did not mean job losses and there was no contradiction between good fiscal policy and a serious labour market policy.

EU heads of state agreed in Dublin last December to the outlines of a stability pact to ensure fiscal discipline after the start of the common European currency. Juncker said it wasn't just the new French government that found the stability pact difficult, but also other countries.
He praised Spain and Italy for their efforts to meet the EMU criteria. Contrary to the views of some, they had made much greater efforts to meet the goals than others in Europe.
